passages.happening:
The chapter opens with a neighbor's lost animal. “If you see your brother’s ox or sheep straying, you must not ignore it; be sure to return it to your brother” (verse 1).

If the owner lives far off, or is not known, the finder is to take the animal home and keep it until the owner comes looking (verse 2). The same holds for ‘his donkey, his cloak, or anything your brother has lost and you have found’ (verse 3).

And if a neighbor's donkey or ox has fallen on the road, “you must not ignore it; you must help him lift it up” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
In a village of small farms an ox or a donkey was a large part of a family's wealth. To lose one could ruin a household.

Three times in four verses the law says, ‘you must not ignore it’. In Hebrew the phrase is, word for word, you shall not hide yourself. It names something everyone knows: the moment of seeing a need and pretending not to have seen it. The law forbids that. Love of neighbor begins with refusing to look away.

The duty costs something. The finder must feed and keep a strange animal, perhaps for a long time, and hand it back without charge. The law does not allow the easy saying that a thing found may be kept.

It reaches past animals to ‘anything’ that is lost.

Exodus gives the same law and applies it to an enemy's animal. Deuteronomy says ‘your brother’. Read together, the two leave no neighbor out.
passages.later:
Exodus pushes the law to its hardest case: “If you encounter your enemy’s stray ox or donkey, you must return it to him” (Exodus 23:4).

Jesus told of two religious men who did what this law forbids. Each saw a wounded man on the road, and each ‘passed by on the other side’ (Luke 10:31-32). A foreigner stopped.

And he pictured God as an owner who goes looking: he ‘does not leave the ninety-nine in the pasture and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it’ (Luke 15:4).
passages.asks: The Hebrew says, do not hide yourself. Ask what need you have recently seen and acted as though you had not. And ask what you are holding that belongs to someone else: a thing borrowed, a debt, or credit for work that was not yours.

passages.t: Clothing, a bird's nest, a railing, and tassels
passages.happening:
A run of short laws follows.

“A woman must not wear men’s clothing, and a man must not wear women’s clothing” (verse 5).

A person who finds a bird's nest with the mother sitting on eggs or chicks may take the young. But ‘be sure to let the mother go’ (verses 6-7).

“If you build a new house, you are to construct a railing around your roof, so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house if someone falls from it” (verse 8).

Three laws forbid mixtures. A vineyard is not to be sown with a second kind of seed. An ox and a donkey are not to be yoked together. Wool and linen are not to be woven into one cloth (verses 9-11).

And: “You are to make tassels on the four corners of the cloak you wear” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
These laws seem to have little in common. Several of them share one idea: care for life, and respect for the order God has made.

The bird's nest. A person may take the eggs or the young for food. The mother must be let go. The law gives no reason beyond a promise that it will go well with the one who keeps it. It teaches restraint toward living things, even small ones that no one would miss.

The railing. Houses in Israel had flat roofs, reached by a ladder or a stair. People dried crops there, slept there in hot weather, and gathered there. A fall was a real danger. The law makes the builder answerable for it. The Hebrew word for the railing is found only here in the Old Testament. The principle reaches far beyond roofs: a person is answerable for a danger he could have foreseen and prevented.

The mixtures. The reasons for these laws are debated. Some see a sign of Israel's own calling to be distinct, since in Genesis 1 God makes each thing according to its kind. Some note that wool and linen together were used in the curtains of the tabernacle and in the priests' clothing, so that the mixture was kept for holy use. The rule about the ox and the donkey also has a plain kindness in it. Animals of different size and strength suffer when they are yoked together.

The tassels. Numbers explains them. They were to be looked at, as a reminder to keep God's commands. Observant Jews still wear them, on the corners of a prayer shawl or an undergarment.

Verse 5, on clothing, stands among these laws about keeping distinct things distinct. The verse gives no reason beyond saying that God detests the practice, and it does not say what it had in view in its own world. These notes argue no application of it today. Nothing here gives anyone a reason for contempt toward any person.
passages.later:
Numbers gives the purpose of the tassels: ‘so that you may remember all the commandments of the LORD’ (Numbers 15:39).

Jesus wore them. A woman who had been ill for twelve years ‘came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His cloak’ (Matthew 9:20).

And Jesus said that God's care reaches as far as this chapter's bird's nest: “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from the will of your Father” (Matthew 10:29).
passages.asks: The builder had to think about who might fall from his roof. Ask what danger you are leaving in place for others because fixing it would cost you. And notice the bird. Ask whether your care for what God has made goes any further than what is useful to you.

passages.happening:
A man marries, comes to hate his wife, and gives her ‘a bad name’. He says that when he married her she was not a virgin (verses 13-14).

Her father and mother bring the proof of her virginity to the elders at the gate, and her father speaks for her (verses 15-17). If she is cleared, the elders punish the man. He is fined a hundred shekels of silver, paid to her father, ‘because this man has given a virgin of Israel a bad name’. And he may never divorce her (verses 18-19).

If the charge is true, the law says she is to be stoned at the door of her father's house (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
The case begins with a husband who has turned against his wife and wants to be rid of her. He chooses the most damaging charge he can make.

In that world a woman's future depended on her standing. A wife sent away under such a charge, true or false, had little hope of another marriage and might be left with no support. The husband's words could destroy her.

So the law gives her a hearing. The case goes to the elders, in public. Her family may bring evidence. The ‘proof’ of verse 17 was the cloth from the wedding night, which the bride's family kept.

If the husband has lied, he is punished and fined. A hundred shekels was a very large sum, twice the bride-price named in verse 29. And he loses the right to divorce her. In a society where a rejected wife could be left with nothing, that guaranteed her support for life. A modern reader may wish she were free to leave such a man. The law is guarding her against being thrown out.

Then the other outcome, in verses 20 and 21. It is severe, and it falls on the woman alone. The hard question below faces it.
passages.later:
Matthew tells of a man who believed he had cause for this very charge and would not use it. Joseph, finding Mary with child, ‘was unwilling to disgrace her publicly’ and ‘resolved to divorce her quietly’ (Matthew 1:19). Matthew calls him a righteous man for it.

When a woman accused of adultery was set in front of Jesus, he sent her accusers away and said, “Then neither do I condemn you,” Jesus declared. “Now go and sin no more” (John 8:11).
passages.hard:
Why does the law say a bride found not to be a virgin must be stoned, and what should a reader make of it?

This is a hard law, and three things about it should be said honestly.

It is uneven. The test falls on the woman. No such test is set for the man.

It was severe. Israel treated marriage as a covenant, and deceit about it as an outrage against the whole community. The penalty reflects that, and it shocks a modern reader.

And it stands beside a real protection. The same law punishes the husband who lies, and it requires a public hearing with evidence before the elders. A woman could not be destroyed by her husband's word alone.

Christians have generally read these penalties as part of Israel's national law, which is not given to the church. The New Testament's own picture is Joseph, who would not shame Mary, and Jesus, who would not condemn.

No one may use these verses to shame, threaten or harm any woman or girl.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law would not let a husband's word alone ruin his wife. Ask whose name you could damage with a word, and whether you have done it. And ask how you treat a person whose past is held against them. Joseph chose not to disgrace, and Jesus chose not to condemn.

passages.t: Adultery, assault, and a woman with no one to save her
passages.happening:
These laws deal with sexual wrongs, case by case.

A man found lying with another man's wife: both are to die (verse 22).

A young woman promised in marriage, and a man who sleeps with her inside a town: both are to be stoned, ‘the young woman because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he has violated his neighbor’s wife’ (verses 23-24).

The same woman, met in open country. “But if the man encounters a betrothed woman in the open country, and he overpowers her and lies with her, only the man who has done this must die. Do nothing to the young woman, because she has committed no sin worthy of death” (verses 25-26). “When he found her in the field, the betrothed woman cried out, but there was no one to save her” (verse 27).

A young woman not promised to anyone. If a man ‘seizes her and lies with her, and they are discovered’, he must pay her father fifty shekels of silver, ‘and she must become his wife because he has violated her. He must not divorce her as long as he lives’ (verses 28-29).

Last, a man is not to marry his father's wife (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
A woman ‘pledged in marriage’ was already legally bound to her future husband, though she still lived in her father's house. That is why the law calls her ‘his neighbor’s wife’.

The center of the passage is verses 25 to 27. A woman is attacked where no one could hear her. The law's ruling is clear. Only the man is guilty. ‘Do nothing to the young woman.’ She ‘has committed no sin’.

The law then makes a comparison that should not be missed. “This case is just like one in which a man attacks his neighbor and murders him.” Rape is set beside murder. The woman stands where a murder victim stands. No one asks a murdered man what he did to bring it on.

And the law assumes that she resisted. There were no witnesses, so nothing could be proved either way. The law gives the benefit of the doubt to her. It says she ‘cried out’. The Hebrew verb is the one used for Israel's cry in Egypt, the cry that God heard.

The case in the town is harder to read. The law takes the woman's silence, where help was near, as a sign that she agreed. A modern reader knows that fear can silence a person anywhere, and that being overpowered does not depend on the place. The law is drawing a rough line for a court with no other evidence. It is not a statement about how any victim ought to behave.

Then verses 28 and 29. They trouble every careful reader, and the hard question below is given to them.

Other law collections of the ancient world also dealt with these matters, often harshly. What stands out here is the ruling for the woman in the field.
passages.later:
The Bible tells the story of a rape in Israel's own royal house. Tamar pleaded, ‘such a thing should never be done in Israel’, but her brother Amnon ‘refused to listen to her, and being stronger, he violated her’ (2 Samuel 13:12, 14). The word she uses for the act is the word this chapter uses for an outrage. The story is told with all its sympathy on her side, and it records her desolation afterward.

A psalm says of the king God promises, “For he will deliver the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no helper” (Psalm 72:12).

Another says, “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit” (Psalm 34:18).
passages.hard:
Do verses 28 and 29 make a woman marry the man who raped her?

That is how the verses read at first sight, and no honest reader is at ease with them.

Readers have said several things.

Some point to the world the law addressed. A woman who was no longer a virgin had little hope of marriage and could be left without support for life. The law makes the man bear the whole cost. He pays a heavy bride-price, and he may never divorce her. On this reading the law's aim is to secure her future and to bind him.

Many note the parallel law in Exodus: “If her father absolutely refuses to give her to him, the man still must pay” (Exodus 22:17). They take that safeguard to apply here too, so that the family could refuse the marriage and still receive the payment.

Scholars also debate the verb in verse 28. It is a different word from the stronger one, ‘overpowers’, in verse 25. Some read it as forcible assault. Others read it as a seduction, closer to the case in Exodus.

None of these removes the difficulty. The law says nothing of what the woman herself wants. That is in the text, and these notes do not explain it away.

Some things are certain. These verses are part of ancient Israel's law and are not given to the church. Nothing here asks any victim to marry, stay with or return to a person who has harmed them. No one may use this passage to press anyone to do so, or to excuse the one who did the harm. Rape is a grave evil. This chapter itself sets it beside murder.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law says of the woman in the field that she cried out and there was no one to save her, and it holds her innocent. Ask whether you believe people who tell you they were harmed, or look first for what they did wrong. And ask who near you is crying out with no one to help, and what it would take for you to be that someone.
